title: Divisor Game
prompt: Alice and Bob take turns playing a game, with Alice starting first. On each player's turn, given the current number `n` on the chalkboard, the player chooses any `x` with `0 < x < n` and `n % x == 0`, and replaces `n` with `n - x`. If a player cannot make a move, they lose the game. Given the starting number `n`, return true if Alice wins the game, assuming both players play optimally, or false if Bob wins.

examples.explanation: Alice picks x = 1, leaving n = 1 for Bob, who has no valid move and loses.
Alice has no valid divisor to pick (no 0 < x < 1), so she loses immediately.
At the maximum constraint boundary, n is even, so Alice can always subtract 1 to hand Bob an odd number and eventually force him into a losing position.

hints: Simulating every possible sequence of moves for both players is expensive — look for a pattern instead by computing small cases by hand.

Define dp[i] = true if the player whose turn it is with the number i on the board wins. dp[i] is true if there exists some valid x such that dp[i - x] is false (leaving the opponent in a losing position).
Try n = 1 through 6 by hand: you'll notice the winner depends only on whether n is even or odd.

solution.approach: This is a game-theory DP problem. Define dp[i] as true if the current player to move, facing number i, wins with optimal play. dp[1] = False (no valid move). For i > 1, dp[i] is True if any divisor x of i lets the player move to i - x where dp[i - x] is False, handing the opponent a losing position. Computing this bottom-up for small i reveals dp[i] is True exactly when i is even: an even number can always subtract 1 (always a valid divisor) to leave an odd number for the opponent, and odd numbers only have odd divisors, so subtracting one always leaves an even number back — meaning the parity flips every turn and starting even guarantees eventually forcing the opponent to 1. This lets the whole problem collapse to a single parity check in O(1), though the DP table view is what proves it.
